justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across the three horizons, starting near 65.2 for the one-day estimate and rising to 67.0 at the one-month mark. The short-term estimate was anchored primarily by recent price momentum and prevailing market microstructure conditions — assuming no major overnight news, prices tend to exhibit mean-reversion or continuation of the near-term trend, so I placed the one-day estimate close to the last observed level with only a slight positive bias. The weekly estimate incorporates a slightly more optimistic drift, reflecting the assumption that underlying fundamentals or trend forces would gradually push prices higher over several sessions. The monthly estimate extends this logic further, assuming that any short-term noise averages out and the dominant directional signal — whatever macro or sector tailwind I was weighting — has time to materialize more fully.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a direct consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. For the one-day interval, I used a relatively tight band of roughly plus or minus two points around the point estimate, reflecting that daily price variation tends to be constrained absent a major catalyst. The one-week interval expands considerably because intraweek news flow, economic data releases, and sentiment shifts are harder to anticipate. By the one-month horizon, the interval spans twenty points, acknowledging that a full month introduces earnings announcements, central bank decisions, geopolitical developments, and shifts in positioning that could materially alter the outcome.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data — a surprise inflation print, a central bank policy shift, or a geopolitical shock — could send prices sharply below the lower bounds, particularly at the monthly horizon. On the upside, a strong risk-on catalyst such as better-than-expected earnings or a dovish policy pivot could drive prices above 77 within a month. Liquidity conditions also matter; in thin markets, price dislocations can be sudden and severe.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals assume a relatively stable volatility regime. If realized volatility spikes — as it can during market stress events — even the one-day interval could prove too narrow. Conversely, if volatility compresses further, the one-month interval might turn out to be overly conservative. These forecasts should be treated as probabilistic guides rather than precise predictions, and they carry meaningful model risk given the inherent difficulty of forecasting prices across any horizon.
